item.title: Accuracy, Reliability, and Efficiency of a MACE Machine-Learning Interatomic Potential for Aspirin: A Reproducible Benchmark for Molecular Simulation
item.description:
Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) can reproduce density functional theory (DFT) energies and forces at a small fraction of the computational cost, yet an average benchmark error is an incomplete measure of their reliability in molecular simulation. This study presents a reproducible workflow that assesses prediction accuracy, error heterogeneity, and dynamical stability together, using aspirin (C9H8O4), a widely used pharmaceutical compound, as an initial molecular benchmark en route to metal-containing systems. A MACE equivariant graph neural network potential is trained on the MD17 dataset and deployed for molecular dynamics through the Atomic Simulation Environment (ASE). Across 210 762 held-out configurations the potential attains a force root-mean-square error of 15.30 meV Å−1, within the published MACE benchmark range, with a validation-to-test generalization gap of 7.6%. Force error correlates positively with configuration energy (Pearson r = 0.51), the carboxyl carbon emerges as the least reliable atomic site, and 90% of force predictions lie within 23.5 meV Å−1 of the DFT reference. Microcanonical simulations conserve total energy and canonical trajectories remain stable, while single-configuration evaluation is approximately four orders of magnitude (a roughly ten-thousand-fold) faster than the corresponding DFT calculation. By combining aggregate accuracy with configuration-and atom-resolved error analysis and explicit dynamical tests, the workflow exposes behavior that a single error metric conceals. The resulting aspirin benchmark establishes a documented baseline for subsequent validation on metal-containing systems and illustrates the value of assessing error distributions and dynamical behavior alongside mean prediction accuracy.

Modupe A. Omoniyi

item.title: Orochi: A Physics-Grounded Python Package for Pair Distribution Function Analysis of Crystalline and Low-Dimensional Materials
item.description:
Atomic pair distribution function (PDF) analysis from X-ray total scattering is a powerful methodology for determining atomic structure and arrangements across crystalline, disordered, nanostructured, and low-dimensional materials on both laboratory and synchrotron instruments. Fundamentally, PDF analysis relies on two core pillars—PDF data reduction from one-dimensional (1D) total scattering profiles and real-space structural modeling—often accompanied in rapid-acquisition experiments by upstream two-dimensional (2D) detector image processing. However, conventional workflows remain fragmented across disconnected software tools, forcing researchers to manually combine multiple programs and preventing the simultaneous optimization of measurement reduction parameters and crystal structure parameters that is standard in X-ray Rietveld refinement. Furthermore, mainstream PDF modeling engines rely on legacy physical approximations: they enforce three-dimensional (3D) periodic boundary conditions (requiring artificial vacuum supercells for 2D nanosheets), treat atomic scattering factors as angle-independent constants (causing peak distortions in compounds with large atomic number contrast), and approximate number density baselines using macroscopic bulk volume assumptions. Here, the open-source, pure-Python architecture of Orochi (version 4.0) is presented, implementing physical calculations from scratch in Python (accelerated via Numba) to unify total scattering data reduction, symmetry-aware crystallographic modeling, and real-space PDF simulation alongside a dedicated high-Q 2D detector processing module within a self-contained Python environment. Originally developed for laboratory total scattering studies of pharmaceutical glasses and deployed as compiled executable (β-version) tools at SPring-8 beamlines, Orochi has been completely redesigned around an externalized parameter management core (orochi.base) in which parameters are stored in standardized Python dictionaries and accessed via hierarchical string addresses. By bringing parameters outside the calculation engines rather than locking them inside built-in optimizers, this architecture allows multiple module instances across data reduction and structural modeling to be optimized simultaneously by modern optimization algorithms, machine learning libraries, and autonomous AI agents. For structural simulation, intra-cell atomic pair vectors are decoupled from lattice translation vectors to natively support arbitrary periodic boundary conditions across 3D crystals, 2D nanosheets, 1D nanowires, and 0D clusters. The simulation engine incorporates the full scattering vector (Q) dependence of atomic form factors, enabling accurate modeling of heavy/light-element oxides and permitting direct instrumental calibration using standard CeO2 powder rather than monoatomic nickel substitutes. Furthermore, a sinc-convolution density formulation is established to accurately reproduce baseline ripples arising from finite Qmin cutoffs in nanostructured systems. Complete mathematical formulations for all reduction and simulation algorithms are consolidated to establish a rigorous foundation for automated crystallographic analysis.

Satoshi Tominaka

item.title: How Metal-to-Linker Ratio and Concentration Govern the Nucleation Mechanism of MOF-5-inspired Crystals: Insights from Multiscale Modeling
A geometry-matched structure generator outperforms basin hopping for silicon cluster global optimisation at fixed relaxation budget
item.description:
In cluster global optimisation the cost is dominated by local relaxations, so the number of relaxations—not wall-clock time—is the natural budget whenever each relaxation is a first-principles or machine-learned potential evaluation. We ask how much of that budget can be saved by the initial structure generator alone. We study a motif-agnostic generator that places each new atom by trilateration at a fixed bond distance from at least three alreadyplaced atoms, subject to a steric admissibility test, and we benchmark it as a drop-in initialiser for Stillinger–Weber silicon clusters with n = 24–60 atoms against three baselines: random structure search, a specialised basin-hopping implementation with single-atom, collective and surface moves and an adaptive step, and a growth-pattern beam search in the spirit of GOALS and GrowPAL. At equal relaxation budget the generator reaches lower minima than specialised basin hopping at every size from n = 32 upward, winning 8/8 paired replicates at n = 48 and n = 60 with complete distributional separation at n = 48, and it beats growth-pattern search in 7/8 paired replicates at both sizes. It also exhibits markedly lower run-to-run variance, and it was the only method to locate the deepest structure found at n = 32, n = 40 and n = 60. The advantage is absent at n = 16, marginal at n = 24, and clean from n = 32; a structural analysis of the resulting minima shows that they are more highly coordinated than the baselines’ but not more tetrahedral in bond angle, so we report the size onset as an unexplained empirical observation rather than attribute it to angular matching. We report the opposite accounting as well: because growth-pattern relaxations start from an already-optimised sub-cluster they are roughly an order of magnitude cheaper in wall-clock, and on equal CPU time the two methods are comparable, while the advantage over basin hopping persists on both accountings.

Chandan Shukla

item.title: Exploration of Particle Swarm Optimization for Parameter Identification in Phase-Field Modeling
item.description:
To address the issue that phase-field (PF) simulation parameter calibration has long relied on manual experience and comparisons with static final-state results, a frame-by-frame parameter identification framework was developed. Three strategies were designed: standard Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), a hybrid PSO incorporating elitism and random reset mechanisms, and Elitist Random Search (ERS). A composite cost function was established, which combined the Dice coefficient and Chamfer distance through a weighting ratio. Hybrid PSO converged earlier and achieved a superior final global optimum cost, demonstrating that this strategy effectively mitigated the risk of entrapment in local optima. Finally, hybrid PSO went through extended validation with longer duration (15s) and larger simulation scale (400 µm × 1700 µm), the average error of the key parameters identified is approximately 2.8%. This work combined frame-by-frame dynamic comparison with hybrid PSO for PF parameter identification for the first time, fundamentally resolving the long-standing problem of degradation in this field.

Hanyu Xu, YiXu Wang, Enzo Liotti, Wenwen Song

item.title: Temperature Mediated Balance of Singlet Fission and Symmetry-Breaking Charge-Transfer in a Polycrystalline Perylene Bisimide Thin Film
item.description:
Singlet fission (SF) and symmetry-breaking charge transfer (SBCT) are competing, and often concurrent, pathways observed in photoexcited organic semiconductor systems: a photoexcited molecule electronically coupled to a neighbor can yield two triplet excited states (SF) or a charge-separated radical ion pair (SBCT). The branching ratio of SF and SBCT is determined largely by the intermolecular electronic coupling, which depends on the relative orientation of neighboring molecules. In a solid thin film, this orientation is defined by the molecular packing, which is typically a static condition established during film formation, and difficult to change with external stimuli. Here, we show that intermolecular coupling in a solid thin film of an asymmetrically substituted perylene bisimide (mXPBI) can be reversibly modulated by temperature alone. Oblique π-stacking in mXPBI produces Davydov-split excitonic states with mixed Coulombic and charge-transfer (CT) coupling character. Temperature-dependent X-ray diffraction reveals modest changes in intermolecular distance and relative molecular orientation. Time-dependent density functional theory calculations demonstrate that these subtle changes to the molecular packing alter the balance between long-range Coulombic and short-range CT coupling, which is expected to influence the competition between SF and SBCT pathways. Transient absorption spectroscopy confirms this prediction, showing that the branching ratio between triplet (SF) and SBCT shifts from approximately 30:70 at 300 K to 50:50 at 100 K. These results demonstrate that excitonic coupling of mXPBI can be reversibly tuned by temperature in the solid state, thereby shifting the balance of competitive photophysical pathways.

Naz Ugur, Debjit Biswas, Daniël Keizer, Chima S. Chibueze, Subhankar Paul, Arka Bikash Dey, Tomasz Marszalek, Adam Kiersnowski, Paul W.M. Blom, Arno Förster, Debangshu Chaudhuri, Charusheela Ramanan
